title: You’ve said yes to things God never asked of you… and somehow stayed silent when He did.
paragraphs: You’ve said yes to things God never asked of you… and somehow stayed silent when He did.

It doesn’t happen loudly. It happens in the quiet negotiations of your heart. You feel the pull, the nudge, the conviction—but you delay. You spiritualize your hesitation. You tell yourself you’re “not ready,” “not qualified,” “not called like that.”
But then Isaiah steps into the scene—and everything you thought was a valid excuse starts collapsing.
The moment wasn’t casual. It wasn’t soft. It wasn’t a motivational whisper.
It was terrifying.
“In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of His robe filled the temple.” (Isaiah 6:1)
This wasn’t a cozy devotional moment. This was holiness—unfiltered, overwhelming, undeniable. The kind that exposes everything in you without saying a word.
Seraphim cried out, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory!” (Isaiah 6:3)
And Isaiah didn’t respond with confidence.
He broke.
“Woe is me! For I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips…” (Isaiah 6:5)
That’s the part most people skip.
Because you want the calling… without the undoing.
You want purpose… without exposure.
You want to be sent… without being purified.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

Isaiah didn’t volunteer from a place of strength.
He surrendered from a place of ruin.
God saw it.
Isaiah’s sin. His unclean lips. His unworthiness. Nothing was hidden.
You knew.
The words you’ve spoken. The compromises you’ve made. The quiet disobedience you’ve justified.
And still—God didn’t cast him away.
A seraphim took a burning coal from the altar and touched Isaiah’s mouth.
“Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.” (Isaiah 6:7)
Read that again.

His guilt… taken away.
His sin… atoned for.
Not ignored. Not excused. Atoned.
This is where everything shifts.
Because before God ever asks, “Whom shall I send?”—He deals with Isaiah’s sin.

Before the mission… comes mercy.
Before the calling… comes cleansing.
And this is where your story intersects with his.
Because that burning coal points forward—to a cross.
To Jesus Christ, who didn’t just touch sin—He carried it.
“He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities… and with His wounds we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:5)
The same God who revealed Isaiah’s sin is the same God who made a way for yours to be forgiven.
Not by your effort. Not by your readiness. Not by your worth.
By grace.
Through faith.
In Jesus.
And only after that…
“Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’” (Isaiah 6:8)
Then.
Not before.
God is not looking for your performance. He’s not scanning for the most impressive, the most polished, the most prepared.
He’s looking for the one who has been undone… and made new.
And Isaiah said something that still echoes through generations:
“Here am I. Send me.”
No hesitation. No conditions. No negotiations.
Why?
Because a man who has truly encountered grace stops clinging to control.

He doesn’t ask, “Where will it take me?”
He doesn’t ask, “Will it be comfortable?”
He doesn’t ask, “What will people think?”
He already knows what he deserved… and what he received instead.
So now the question turns toward you.

You’ve heard truth before.
You’ve felt conviction before.
You’ve had moments where God was clearly calling… and you chose silence.
But what if this is your Isaiah 6 moment?
What if the delay ends here?
Not because you suddenly feel ready—but because you finally understand grace.
He cleanses the called.
Two paths sit in front of you right now.
One where you keep analyzing, delaying, holding back pieces of your life while still calling yourself “available.”
And one where you surrender fully—where “Here am I” actually means something.
Where obedience replaces excuses.
Where repentance isn’t a one-time feeling but a lifestyle.
Where Jesus is no longer just someone you believe in—but Someone you follow.
That’s not emotion. That’s conviction.
Say it—don’t type it perfectly, just say it honestly:
Not the polished version of you. The real one.
If this hit something deep, don’t keep it to yourself. Let this interrupt their silence the way it just interrupted yours.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—not just inspired, but discipled—there’s a place for that:
Because “Here am I” is just the beginning.
